newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan brewers froth over rising malt import costs.
newsitem.headline: Japan brewers froth over rising malt import costs.

text.p: Japanese brewers are foaming at the mouth at the rising cost of importing malt for beer production and are considering cutting longer-term deals to reduce expenses, company officials say.
Japan, the world's fifth-largest beer producer in 1995 after the United States, China, Germany and Brazil, produced 6.80 million kilolitres (1.5 billion gallons) of beer, down 5.4 percent from 1994.
Kirin Brewery Co Ltd, Japan's largest beer producer, blamed the weak yen for a big rise in the cost of importing malt.

"Our malt import costs for the 1995 crop rose by five billion yen ($45.4 million) from 1994, mainly because of the yen's steep drop," said Hiroyuki Kamiya, general manager of Kirin's purchasing department.
Nearly 90 percent of Japan's imports of malt for brewing beer, made from barley steeped in water and allowed to germinate, comes from Europe, North America and Australia.
Local industry officials say the circumstances surrounding malt imports are becoming more difficult for them.
Kirin usually buys about 350,000 tonnes of malt a year, and its average import costs rose to 63,000 yen ($572) a tonne for the 1995 crop from 48,000 yen ($436) for the 1994 crop.
"But we can't resort to raising beer prices," Kamiya said. "Competition by local beer makers for a larger share of the market is intensifying and imported beers are increasing."

Asahi Breweries Ltd, the second-largest brewer in Japan, is facing a similar dilemma. The company said its malt import cost for the 1995 crop rose by 3.6 billion yen ($32.7 million) compared with the year before.
"The higher malt cost doesn't mean any immediate supply shortage," said Tokutaro Yoshioka, general manager of its raw materials department. "But rising malt prices are a negative factor."
To cope with higher malt prices, Japanese brewers are considering long-term contracts with overseas producers instead of annual deals.
This year Kirin Brewery will buy about 150,000 tonnes or 43 percent of its malt imports through three-year deals.
"The share of the long-term import contracts in 1995 was 34 percent. Instead of fixing a quantity of imports, we may be able to set lower purchasing prices," Kirin's Kamiya said.
Shipping malt to ports in Singapore and South Korea is seen as another way to cut costs, industry officials said.

"Domestic transport costs in Japan are rising further. The irony is that it's less expensive to transship European malts in Singapore to smaller-sized vessels and then send them to local ports here," a senior official at a major brewer said.
Japanese brewers are also closely watching the European Union's policy on malt export refunds and will shift to cheaper malt from North America unless the EU raises export refunds.

The EU on Thursday set a daily refund of 32.50 Ecus per tonne for the export of unroasted malt in the 1996/97 season, European grain traders said last week. The refund is valid for 11 months, including September.
"Our bottom line is that the figure is still lower than expected. Unless the refund is raised further, we may be forced to shift to cheaper malt from North America," the senior brewery official said.
